scenes.text: It's October 1929, and the New York stock market is falling apart.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Wall Street outside the New York Stock Exchange during the October 1929 crash: classical columns, overcast sky, papers blowing on the pavement, 1920s cars parked

scenes.text: Men who were millionaires on Monday are begging for cab fare by Thursday.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Wall Street outside the New York Stock Exchange during the October 1929 crash: classical columns, overcast sky, papers blowing on the pavement, 1920s cars parked

scenes.text: And in a quiet office on Fifth Avenue, you are smiling.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: private trading office on Fifth Avenue, 1929: wall-size green chalkboard of stock prices, stock ticker machine with paper tape, Art Deco desk, tall window over Manhattan

scenes.text: Because months ago, you bet that all of this would happen.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: private trading office on Fifth Avenue, 1929: wall-size green chalkboard of stock prices, stock ticker machine with paper tape, Art Deco desk, tall window over Manhattan

scenes.text: By the end of it, you'll be about a hundred million dollars richer.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: private trading office on Fifth Avenue, 1929: wall-size green chalkboard of stock prices, stock ticker machine with paper tape, Art Deco desk, tall window over Manhattan

scenes.text: Eleven years later, you'll die alone in a hotel cloakroom, calling yourself a failure.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: elegant Manhattan hotel bar, 1940: dark wood bar counter, brass rail, mirrors, leather stools, a cloakroom door at the side, evening lamplight

scenes.text: So how do you win that much, and still lose?
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: elegant Manhattan hotel bar, 1940: dark wood bar counter, brass rail, mirrors, leather stools, a cloakroom door at the side, evening lamplight

scenes.text: By the end, you'll know the one money rule that got you here.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: And whether it still works today.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: But to get here, we have to go back.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: It's 1877, and you're born in Shrewsbury, Massachusetts.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Your name is Jesse Lauriston Livermore, and your family is very poor.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Keep count of three things: the money, the wives, and the times you go broke.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You're going to need more fingers for that last one.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Your family moves to a farm in Acton, where the soil mostly grows rocks.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You're a quick child: you can read and write at three and a half.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: And you're especially good at one thing: numbers.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In 1891, at fourteen, your father pulls you out of school to work the farm.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You do not want to spend your life walking behind a plow.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: So your mother helps you run away.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: She gives you five dollars for the road.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Remember that five dollars.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You walk out with one suit and five dollars, heading for Boston.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Within days, you get a job at the PaineWebber brokerage.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Boston brokerage office, 1891: huge blackboard of stock prices along one wall, wooden ladder, telegraph sounder on a desk, chalk and rags

scenes.text: Your job title is board boy, which is exactly what it sounds like.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Boston brokerage office, 1891: huge blackboard of stock prices along one wall, wooden ladder, telegraph sounder on a desk, chalk and rags

scenes.text: Prices arrive by telegraph, and you chalk them onto a giant board.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Boston brokerage office, 1891: huge blackboard of stock prices along one wall, wooden ladder, telegraph sounder on a desk, chalk and rags

scenes.text: The pay is five dollars a week.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Boston brokerage office, 1891: huge blackboard of stock prices along one wall, wooden ladder, telegraph sounder on a desk, chalk and rags

scenes.text: And you notice something the grown men around you miss.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Boston brokerage office, 1891: huge blackboard of stock prices along one wall, wooden ladder, telegraph sounder on a desk, chalk and rags

scenes.text: Prices move in patterns, like the same tune played again and again.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Boston brokerage office, 1891: huge blackboard of stock prices along one wall, wooden ladder, telegraph sounder on a desk, chalk and rags

scenes.text: So you start writing them down in a little notebook.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Boston brokerage office, 1891: huge blackboard of stock prices along one wall, wooden ladder, telegraph sounder on a desk, chalk and rags

scenes.text: Remember that notebook.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Boston brokerage office, 1891: huge blackboard of stock prices along one wall, wooden ladder, telegraph sounder on a desk, chalk and rags

scenes.text: The crash that makes you a hundred million is thirty-eight years away.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In 1892, a friend talks you into trying a bucket shop.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Boston bucket shop, 1890s: narrow betting parlor, chalk quotation board, stock ticker machine under a glass dome, wooden counter with a cashier's window, spittoons

scenes.text: A bucket shop: a parlor where you bet on stock prices without buying any stock.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Boston bucket shop, 1890s: narrow betting parlor, chalk quotation board, stock ticker machine under a glass dome, wooden counter with a cashier's window, spittoons

scenes.text: It's like betting on a horse race without ever owning a horse.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Boston bucket shop, 1890s: narrow betting parlor, chalk quotation board, stock ticker machine under a glass dome, wooden counter with a cashier's window, spittoons

scenes.text: You bet five dollars on a railroad, the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Boston bucket shop, 1890s: narrow betting parlor, chalk quotation board, stock ticker machine under a glass dome, wooden counter with a cashier's window, spittoons

scenes.text: Two days later, you collect three dollars and twelve cents in profit.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Boston bucket shop, 1890s: narrow betting parlor, chalk quotation board, stock ticker machine under a glass dome, wooden counter with a cashier's window, spittoons

scenes.text: It's the first money you've ever made without moving a single rock.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Boston bucket shop, 1890s: narrow betting parlor, chalk quotation board, stock ticker machine under a glass dome, wooden counter with a cashier's window, spittoons

scenes.text: At sixteen, you quit your job to trade full time.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Boston bucket shop, 1890s: narrow betting parlor, chalk quotation board, stock ticker machine under a glass dome, wooden counter with a cashier's window, spittoons

scenes.text: Your one law: bet only on what the price tape shows, never on tips.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Boston bucket shop, 1890s: narrow betting parlor, chalk quotation board, stock ticker machine under a glass dome, wooden counter with a cashier's window, spittoons

scenes.text: Remember that.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Boston bucket shop, 1890s: narrow betting parlor, chalk quotation board, stock ticker machine under a glass dome, wooden counter with a cashier's window, spittoons

scenes.text: By 1894, you're making about two hundred dollars a week.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: That's forty times your old salary, and you're seventeen.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Boston's bucket shops start calling you the Boy Plunger.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You go home and hand your mother a thousand dollars.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: That's her five dollars, two hundred times over.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: She calls it gambling.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You call it speculating: betting on where a price goes next, with a reason.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: By 1897, the Boston bucket shops have had quite enough of you.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Boston bucket shop, 1890s: narrow betting parlor, chalk quotation board, stock ticker machine under a glass dome, wooden counter with a cashier's window, spittoons

scenes.text: You've taken about ten thousand dollars from them in three years.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Boston bucket shop, 1890s: narrow betting parlor, chalk quotation board, stock ticker machine under a glass dome, wooden counter with a cashier's window, spittoons

scenes.text: So they ban you, because a casino hates nothing more than a winner.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Boston bucket shop, 1890s: narrow betting parlor, chalk quotation board, stock ticker machine under a glass dome, wooden counter with a cashier's window, spittoons

scenes.text: One firm, Haight and Freese, still takes your bets, but quietly tilts the odds.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: It charges you more on every trade, hoping you'll finally lose.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You keep winning anyway.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: On September 14, 1900, you step off the train in New York.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You bring ten thousand dollars and a great deal of confidence.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: At a real brokerage, you turn it into fifty thousand in five days.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The crash that makes you a hundred million is now twenty-nine years away.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: That October, you marry Nettie Jordan of Indianapolis, after knowing her a few weeks.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You buy her beautiful jewelry, because you're rich now.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Remember that jewelry.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In May 1901, you bet hard against the market with borrowed money.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The market goes up instead, and you lose everything.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: That bet has a name, and one day it will make you famous: short selling.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Imagine your neighbor lends you his bicycle for a month.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small-town bicycle shop, 1900: tall safety bicycles in a row, wheels hanging on the wall, workbench with tools, sunny shop window

scenes.text: You sell it today for one hundred dollars.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small-town bicycle shop, 1900: tall safety bicycles in a row, wheels hanging on the wall, workbench with tools, sunny shop window

scenes.text: Next week, the same bicycle costs sixty, so you buy one.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small-town bicycle shop, 1900: tall safety bicycles in a row, wheels hanging on the wall, workbench with tools, sunny shop window

scenes.text: You give it back to your neighbor and keep forty dollars.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small-town bicycle shop, 1900: tall safety bicycles in a row, wheels hanging on the wall, workbench with tools, sunny shop window

scenes.text: That's short selling: borrow a stock, sell it, buy it back cheaper later.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small-town bicycle shop, 1900: tall safety bicycles in a row, wheels hanging on the wall, workbench with tools, sunny shop window

scenes.text: But if the price rises instead, you lose, with no ceiling on the loss.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small-town bicycle shop, 1900: tall safety bicycles in a row, wheels hanging on the wall, workbench with tools, sunny shop window

scenes.text: And with borrowed money, even a small move the wrong way wipes you out.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small-town bicycle shop, 1900: tall safety bicycles in a row, wheels hanging on the wall, workbench with tools, sunny shop window

scenes.text: Which is exactly what just happened to you.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small-town bicycle shop, 1900: tall safety bicycles in a row, wheels hanging on the wall, workbench with tools, sunny shop window

scenes.text: You ask Nettie to pawn her jewelry, so you can trade again.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Pawn: hand it to a shop for a loan; miss a payment, it's gone.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: She says no.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The marriage never quite recovers.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You borrow two thousand dollars from a broker friend, Ed Hutton, and leave town.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In the bucket shops of St. Louis, you build it back up.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Then a bet on Northern Pacific railroad stock turns ten thousand into half a million.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You're twenty-four, and you've already been broke twice.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In April 1906, you get a strange feeling about Union Pacific, a railroad stock.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Nothing looks wrong, but you bet against it anyway.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The next day, an earthquake destroys San Francisco.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: San Francisco street after the 1906 earthquake: collapsed brick buildings, cracked cobbles, smoke rising in the distance, cable car tracks

scenes.text: Union Pacific's railroad runs straight into that city, and its stock collapses.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: San Francisco street after the 1906 earthquake: collapsed brick buildings, cracked cobbles, smoke rising in the distance, cable car tracks

scenes.text: You make about two hundred and fifty thousand dollars.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Everybody calls it luck. You call it reading the tape.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Then Ed Hutton talks you out of a rebound bet, and you lose forty thousand.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: It's October 1907, and New York's banks are running out of cash.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The cost of borrowing money for one night shoots past one hundred percent.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: And you are short on almost everything.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In a single day, you make one million dollars.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Then a message arrives from J. P. Morgan, the most powerful banker in America.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Morgan asks you to stop selling, before you break the whole market.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Being asked a favor by Morgan is not something that happens twice.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You agree, flip around, and start buying instead.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: When stocks bounce back, you're worth about three million dollars.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You buy a two-hundred-thousand-dollar yacht, a private railroad car, and an apartment.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The crash that makes you a hundred million is twenty-two years away.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In 1908, you meet Teddy Price, a famous cotton trader.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: He is charming, he is confident, and he is very sure about cotton.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: He says prices are going up, so you buy, and buy, and buy.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: That's a tip: the one thing you swore never to trade on.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: What you don't know: Price is secretly selling.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Cotton falls, and you hold on while it falls further.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: New York Cotton Exchange trading floor, 1908: octagonal trading ring, cotton bales and sample tables, big price board, tall arched windows

scenes.text: By the end, most of your three million is gone.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: New York Cotton Exchange trading floor, 1908: octagonal trading ring, cotton bales and sample tables, big price board, tall arched windows

scenes.text: The tape told you to sell, but you listened to a man instead.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: New York Cotton Exchange trading floor, 1908: octagonal trading ring, cotton bales and sample tables, big price board, tall arched windows

scenes.text: Or as the book about you will later put it:
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: New York Cotton Exchange trading floor, 1908: octagonal trading ring, cotton bales and sample tables, big price board, tall arched windows

scenes.text: There is only one side to the stock market: the right side.
scenes.speaker: narrator

quote.text: There is only one side to the stock market... the right side.

scenes.bgIdea: New York Cotton Exchange trading floor, 1908: octagonal trading ring, cotton bales and sample tables, big price board, tall arched windows

scenes.text: For years after that, nothing you try quite works.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In 1915, you file for bankruptcy.
scenes.speaker: narrator

paper.text: PETITION IN BANKRUPTCY: J. L. LIVERMORE

scenes.text: Bankruptcy: a court agrees you can't pay, so your creditors must stop chasing you.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You're thirty-seven, and you are starting over from nothing.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: A broker agrees to let you trade again, on credit.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You wait, and wait, for the one trade the tape is begging you to make.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In 1917, you finally make it big again.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You pay back every creditor, even though the court says you don't have to.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Some of them probably count the money twice, out of pure surprise.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: That same year, you and Nettie divorce.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Neither of you ever really got past that jewelry.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Around 1918, you quietly corner the cotton market.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: New York Cotton Exchange trading floor, 1908: octagonal trading ring, cotton bales and sample tables, big price board, tall arched windows

scenes.text: Corner: owning so much of something that everyone else must buy it from you.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: New York Cotton Exchange trading floor, 1908: octagonal trading ring, cotton bales and sample tables, big price board, tall arched windows

scenes.text: Yes, the same cotton that broke you ten years ago.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: New York Cotton Exchange trading floor, 1908: octagonal trading ring, cotton bales and sample tables, big price board, tall arched windows

scenes.text: President Woodrow Wilson gets involved, and you agree to sell at no profit.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Asked why you did it, you reportedly answer:
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: To see if I could, Mr. President.
scenes.speaker: narrator

quote.text: To see if I could, Mr. President.

scenes.text: In December 1918, you marry Dorothy Wendt, a former Ziegfeld showgirl.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Ziegfeld: the most famous chorus line on Broadway.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You're past forty, and she's in her early twenties.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You have two sons, Jesse Junior and Paul.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You spend about three and a half million dollars on a house in Great Neck.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In 1923, a book about you comes out.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Its title: Reminiscences of a Stock Operator.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The internet says it's your autobiography.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: It isn't: a journalist, Edwin Lefevre, wrote it after interviewing you.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: And the hero isn't even called Jesse Livermore: he's Larry Livingston.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Close enough that everyone on Wall Street knows exactly who it is.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In it, you say there is nothing new in Wall Street.
scenes.speaker: narrator

quote.text: There is nothing new in Wall Street.

scenes.text: Its most famous line is about patience.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: It never was my thinking that made the big money. It always was my sitting.
scenes.speaker: narrator

quote.text: It never was my thinking that made the big money... It always was my sitting.

scenes.text: The crash that makes you a hundred million is six years away.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: By early 1929, everyone is buying stocks, many with borrowed money.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Wall Street outside the New York Stock Exchange during the October 1929 crash: classical columns, overcast sky, papers blowing on the pavement, 1920s cars parked

scenes.text: Your price notes tell you prices are climbing on fewer and fewer buyers.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: private trading office on Fifth Avenue, 1929: wall-size green chalkboard of stock prices, stock ticker machine with paper tape, Art Deco desk, tall window over Manhattan

scenes.text: So you quietly bet against the market, through more than a hundred brokers.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: private trading office on Fifth Avenue, 1929: wall-size green chalkboard of stock prices, stock ticker machine with paper tape, Art Deco desk, tall window over Manhattan

scenes.text: That way, nobody can see how big your bet really is.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: private trading office on Fifth Avenue, 1929: wall-size green chalkboard of stock prices, stock ticker machine with paper tape, Art Deco desk, tall window over Manhattan

scenes.text: By spring, you're down more than six million dollars on paper.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: private trading office on Fifth Avenue, 1929: wall-size green chalkboard of stock prices, stock ticker machine with paper tape, Art Deco desk, tall window over Manhattan

scenes.text: Every instinct says give up. You sit.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: private trading office on Fifth Avenue, 1929: wall-size green chalkboard of stock prices, stock ticker machine with paper tape, Art Deco desk, tall window over Manhattan

scenes.text: And then it's October 1929 again, and the floor gives way.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Wall Street outside the New York Stock Exchange during the October 1929 crash: classical columns, overcast sky, papers blowing on the pavement, 1920s cars parked

scenes.text: In two days, the market falls almost a quarter.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In your office, bets you made months ago pay off all at once.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: private trading office on Fifth Avenue, 1929: wall-size green chalkboard of stock prices, stock ticker machine with paper tape, Art Deco desk, tall window over Manhattan

scenes.text: You clear about one hundred million dollars.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: That's almost two billion dollars in today's money.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The newspapers call you the Great Bear of Wall Street.
scenes.speaker: narrator

paper.text: THE GREAT BEAR OF WALL STREET

scenes.text: A bear: someone who bets that prices will fall.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The internet says you caused the crash.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You didn't: one man can't sink a market that big, only see it coming.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: But angry people skip the fine print, and you get death threats.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: So you hire an armed bodyguard to walk you to work.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: And then, slowly, the money starts leaking out of your life.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In 1932, Dorothy divorces you, reportedly for a ten million dollar settlement.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In 1933, you marry Harriet Metz Noble, a singer from Omaha.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You are her fifth husband.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The internet says all four husbands before you took their own lives.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Records show at least two did, including one after the 1929 crash.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In 1934, Washington creates the SEC: a new referee for Wall Street.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Your secret, giant bets now come with rules and paperwork.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: private trading office on Fifth Avenue, 1929: wall-size green chalkboard of stock prices, stock ticker machine with paper tape, Art Deco desk, tall window over Manhattan

scenes.text: That same year, you go bankrupt again.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You list eighty-four thousand dollars in assets, and two and a half million in debts.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In 1935, Dorothy, drunk, shoots your son Jesse Junior.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: He survives.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You never fully recover from that year.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In 1937, the tax office still sends you a bill for eight hundred thousand dollars.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In 1939, you open a business selling your trading system to others.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: And Jesse Junior suggests you write a book.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In March 1940, it comes out: How to Trade in Stocks.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: It's built on the habit you started at fourteen, in that little notebook.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Patterns, rules and prices, written down and studied for almost fifty years.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: But the world is busy with a war, and the book sells poorly.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: It's Thanksgiving Day, November 28, 1940.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: elegant Manhattan hotel bar, 1940: dark wood bar counter, brass rail, mirrors, leather stools, a cloakroom door at the side, evening lamplight

scenes.text: You sit at the bar of the Sherry-Netherland hotel in Manhattan.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: elegant Manhattan hotel bar, 1940: dark wood bar counter, brass rail, mirrors, leather stools, a cloakroom door at the side, evening lamplight

scenes.text: Then you walk into the cloakroom, and take your own life.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: elegant Manhattan hotel bar, 1940: dark wood bar counter, brass rail, mirrors, leather stools, a cloakroom door at the side, evening lamplight

scenes.text: You are sixty-three.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: elegant Manhattan hotel bar, 1940: dark wood bar counter, brass rail, mirrors, leather stools, a cloakroom door at the side, evening lamplight

scenes.text: You leave Harriet an eight-page note.
scenes.speaker: narrator

paper.text: I AM TIRED OF FIGHTING... I AM A FAILURE.

scenes.text: It says: I am tired of fighting. I am a failure.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The internet says you died broke.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Not quite: most accounts put your estate at about five million dollars.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Much of it reportedly sat in trusts you set up in the good years.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: So how does the man who won a hundred million call himself a failure?
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You broke your own rules, again and again: tips, borrowed money, impatience.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: And your rules were the only part of the market you could control.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Here is the money rule from your life.
scenes.speaker: narrator

paper.text: MONEY RULE: NEVER BREAK YOUR OWN RULES

scenes.text: Decide your rules while you're calm, and follow them while you're scared.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: private trading office on Fifth Avenue, 1929: wall-size green chalkboard of stock prices, stock ticker machine with paper tape, Art Deco desk, tall window over Manhattan

scenes.text: Say your rule is: never invest money you'll need within five years.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In 2022, big tech stocks as a group fall about a third.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: If your rule held, you wait, and by 2024 they've climbed back.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: If you broke it and need that cash now, you sell at the bottom.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: But rules fail too: buyers at the 1929 peak waited twenty-five years to break even.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Wall Street outside the New York Stock Exchange during the October 1929 crash: classical columns, overcast sky, papers blowing on the pavement, 1920s cars parked

scenes.text: And you knew every rule by heart, and still couldn't keep them.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: elegant Manhattan hotel bar, 1940: dark wood bar counter, brass rail, mirrors, leather stools, a cloakroom door at the side, evening lamplight

scenes.text: Writing a rule down is easy. Keeping it is the whole job.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Boston brokerage office, 1891: huge blackboard of stock prices along one wall, wooden ladder, telegraph sounder on a desk, chalk and rags

scenes.text: The market never tests what you know. It tests what you'll do.
scenes.speaker: narrator

meta.thumbnail: A 1929 trading floor in chaos: a giant chalkboard of crashing stock prices, ticker tape flying, panicked brokers in the background; text: 'SHORTED 1929'
meta.description:
It's 1929. Wall Street is collapsing, and you just made a hundred million dollars betting on it.
Eleven years later, you call yourself a failure. This is the life of Jesse Livermore.

A comedic dramatization of documented history. Quotes marked as from 'Reminiscences of a Stock Operator' come from Edwin Lefevre's 1923 book about a lightly fictionalized Livermore.
This video discusses suicide. If you are struggling, in the US you can call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline); elsewhere, contact your local emergency or crisis line.
General education only, not financial advice.

Sources:
- Jesse Livermore, Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_Livermore
- Edwin Lefevre, Reminiscences of a Stock Operator (1923)
- Jesse Livermore, How to Trade in Stocks (1940)
- MoneyWeek profile: https://moneyweek.com/30284/profile-of-jesse-livermore-worlds-greatest-trader-23100
factCheck: Born July 26, 1877, Shrewsbury MA; moved to Acton as a child; read and wrote at 3.5 (Wikipedia).
1891 at 14: pulled from school by father, ran away with mother's blessing and $5; PaineWebber board boy at $5/week (Wikipedia).
1892 first bucket shop bet: $5 on Chicago, Burlington & Quincy, $3.12 profit; 'two days later' from Reminiscences.
1893-94 about $200/week, nicknamed Boy Plunger; $1,000 to mother; 1895-97 about $10,000, barred by Boston bucket shops; Haight & Freese 1898-1900 (Wikipedia).

Sept 14, 1900 to New York at 23 with $10,000; $50,000 in five days at Harris, Hutton; married Nettie Jordan Oct 1900; May 1901 lost all on margin short; borrowed $2,000 from E. F. Hutton; St. Louis; Northern Pacific $10K to $500K in 1901 (Wikipedia).
1906 Union Pacific short before San Francisco earthquake: +$250,000; Hutton talked him out of rebound, -$40,000 (Wikipedia). Running money totals on the counter are rough estimates.
1907: call money rates above 100% (widely reported, about 125% on Oct 24); $1M in one day; Morgan asked him to stop; net worth about $3M; $200,000 yacht, rail car, apartment (Wikipedia).
1908 cotton: Theodore H. 'Teddy' Price (called Percy Thomas in Reminiscences) urged buying while secretly selling (Wikipedia).

1915 bankruptcy; 1917 repaid creditors (Reminiscences; widely repeated). Nettie divorce Oct 1917. Cotton corner after WWI and Wilson quote 'To see if I could, Mr. President' are on Wikipedia but thinly sourced: DISPUTED. 'Around 1918' is approximate.
Married Dorothy Fox Wendt Dec 2, 1918, former Ziegfeld girl aged about 22-23; sons Jesse Jr (1919) and Paul (1922); $3.5M Great Neck house (Wikipedia).

1929: shorts via 100+ brokers, down over $6M by spring, netted about $100M; 'Great Bear of Wall Street'; death threats, armed bodyguard (Wikipedia). Today's value ~ $1.9B using CPI x19 (1929 to 2026, approx).
Dow fell 12.8% Oct 28 and 11.7% Oct 29, 1929: about 23% in two days.
Divorce Sept 1932, reported $10M settlement; married Harriet Metz Noble March 28, 1933, her fifth husband; at least two prior husbands died by suicide (Wikipedia).
SEC created 1934; bankruptcy 1934 with $84,000 assets, $2.5M debts; 1935 Dorothy shot Jesse Jr (non-fatal); $800,000 tax bill paid in 1937 (Wikipedia).
1939 advisory business; How to Trade in Stocks, March 1940, suggested by Jesse Jr, sold poorly (Wikipedia).
Died Nov 28, 1940 (Thanksgiving) at the Sherry-Netherland hotel, aged 63; eight-page note to Harriet ('I am tired of fighting', 'I am a failure') (Wikipedia).
Estate about $5M, partly in trusts: repeated in secondary sources (MoneyWeek etc.), no probate record found: DISPUTED.
2022: Nasdaq Composite fell about 33%; recovered its prior high in 2024. Dow regained its 1929 peak in November 1954.
sources: Edwin Lefevre, Reminiscences of a Stock Operator (1923): 'There is nothing new in Wall Street.'; 'There is only one side to the stock market; and it is not the bull side or the bear side, but the right side.'; 'It never was my thinking that made the big money for me. It always was my sitting.' (narrator Larry Livingston, modelled on Livermore)
'To see if I could, Mr. President.' as quoted on https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_Livermore (thinly sourced)
Suicide note excerpts as quoted on https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_Livermore
